newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia to apply garment export quotas.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia to apply garment export quotas.

text.p: Cambodian Commerce Minister Cham Prasidh on Tuesday announced internal quotas and tighter controls on the garment sector, the country's fastest-growing industry.

The new rules were needed to combat the growing problem of unscrupulous companies labelling foreign goods as made in Cambodia to take advantage of the country's preferential trade status, Cham Prasidh told garment makers at a conference.

"We have to be very cautious because some countries would exploit the Cambodian name and send tee-shirts, apparel, etc... and claim those goods are of Cambodian origin," he said, adding that the problem could spiral out of control and cause Cambodia to exceed future trade quotas with other nations.
The regulations would require Cambodia's 35 garment factories to negotiate production ceilings with the government and certify their goods under U.S. rules, he said.

This would enable Cambodia to monitor its exports and more easily identify illegally marked shipments, Cham Prasidh said. He added that while there were no current U.S. limits on garments, "apparel is a very sensitive sector for the U.S".
Control of exports would be crucial in obtaining Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) trade status with the United States, he said.
Such status would specify that Cambodia cannot exceed 50 percent of total U.S. imports in any one category, or top $82.5 million, in any one year.
Cambodia was awarded Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trade status earlier this month. Cham Prasidh said he hoped Washington would grant GSP status by the end of the year.
MFN lowers trade tariffs to the levels of most trading partners, while GSP provides the lowest possible tariff rates on many products, although it excludes textiles and garments.

Van Sou Ieng, chairman of the Cambodian Garment Manufacturers' Association, said he was not concerned about the quotas, which he said were aimed at monitoring rather than regulating $50 million in annual exports.
"We would like to have the rules implemented so honest industries will not be affected by (dishonest ones)," he said.
